name: Skagen
title: Skagen UTM: Ship Gauging at the Skaw Anchorage and Harbour
description: Ship thickness gauging off Skagen and in the harbour: tankers and bulk carriers at the Skaw anchorage, fishing vessels and coasters, decks and ballast tanks.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement off the Skaw and in Skagen Harbour
intro: Skagen, at the very tip of Jutland where the Skagerrak meets the Kattegat, serves ships in two ways. Offshore, its anchorages hold tankers, bulk carriers and container ships stopping to bunker, take stores, change crew, transfer cargo or wait for orders on their way into or out of the Baltic. In the harbour, one of Denmark's largest fishing fleets shares the quays with coasters, cruise ships and a shipyard. Atlantis flies its technicians in from India to these ships, boarding by launch at anchor or by gangway alongside.

highlights.h: Launch work at the Skaw anchorages
highlights.p: Ships anchored off Skagen for bunkers, stores or orders can be boarded by launch through their agent. A prepared scope of deck plating, air pipes, hatch coamings and a handful of ballast tanks fits the hours a ship spends at anchor before sailing on.

Tankers lying off Skagen while they wait for orders or complete ship-to-ship transfers can stay for days. That gives a prospective buyer, charterer or owner the chance to gauge ballast tanks and deck structure without diverting the ship into a port.

highlights.h: Fishing vessels at their home port
highlights.p: Skagen's pelagic and demersal fleet lands catches in the harbour and lies alongside between trips. Steel hulls, refrigerated sea-water tanks and decks worn by fishing gear are best measured while a vessel is idle, often in the weeks before a season opens.

port.h: Skagen: anchorage and harbour where the Skagerrak meets the Kattegat
p: Skagen lies at the northern point of Jutland, close to Grenen, the long sand spit where the waters of the Skagerrak and the Kattegat meet. Every ship entering or leaving the Baltic through the Danish straits rounds this corner, and the sheltered water off the town has long served as an anchorage for vessels waiting for weather, orders, a berth further in or a cargo deal to close. Shelter depends on the wind. In westerly weather the anchorages on the Kattegat side of the point lie in the lee of the land, while strong easterly winds expose them and make boarding by launch harder. The anchorage area is busy throughout the year with tankers, bulk carriers, container ships and vehicle carriers, and at times the ships at anchor outnumber those in the harbour many times over.

Marine fuel suppliers deliver bunkers by barge off Skagen, which has made it one of the established bunkering points in northern Europe for ships trading between the Baltic and the rest of the world. Ships use the stop for crew changes, provisions and spare parts at the same time, so agents in the town are used to arranging launches and boarding at short notice. Ship-to-ship transfers of oil cargoes also take place in the area under Danish rules, and some tankers lie off Skagen for extended periods. The result is a steady concentration of deep-sea ships from many owners and flags, a short launch ride from a harbour that most of them will never enter, and a regular source of short-notice inspection requests.

The harbour itself is a different world. Skagen is one of Denmark's largest fishing ports, with pelagic trawlers landing herring, mackerel and sprat for human consumption and for the fishmeal plant, and demersal vessels landing for the fish auction. A shipyard in the harbour builds and repairs fishing vessels and other specialised craft, and the port has been extended with deeper quays that now take cruise ships in summer as well as coasters and project cargo. The fishing calendar shapes the year: vessels are busiest while the herring and mackerel fisheries are open and lie alongside between them, which is when owners plan surveys, refits and gauging. Winter storms can close the anchorages to launch work for days, but they rarely stop work inside the harbour.

facilities.h: Where gauging is practical at Skagen
p: At the anchorage, all work is done by launch. The ship's agent books the boat, the team climbs a pilot or accommodation ladder, and the kit is limited to what technicians can carry up it, so the scope and the equipment are settled before the boat leaves the harbour. Ballast tanks must already be emptied, ventilated and certified safe for entry by the crew, because a few hours at anchor leave no time to prepare them once the team is aboard. Work stops whenever the swell makes the ladder unsafe, which is why the readings that matter most are always placed first on the list.

Inside the harbour, the shipyard Karstensens Skibsværft builds and repairs fishing vessels and other specialised craft, and vessels under repair there can be gauged alongside or out of the water. Large merchant ships do not dock at Skagen; those that need a dry dock after an anchorage stop usually go to Ørskov Yard in Frederikshavn, to Fayard on Funen, or to yards in Poland, Germany or Norway. Coasters and cargo ships at the commercial quays can be measured while they work cargo, and fishing vessels between trips at their regular berths in the fishing harbour.
list: Skagen anchorages — deck, hatch coaming, air-pipe and ballast tank gauging by launch on ships stopping for bunkers, stores or crew change.
Tankers waiting or transferring cargo off Skagen — ballast tank, void space and deck gauging over longer stays, within the ship's gas-safety rules.
Karstensens Skibsværft — hull, deck and tank measurement on fishing vessels and specialised craft in for repair.
Fishing harbour berths — shell plating, refrigerated sea-water tank and fish-hold gauging on trawlers between trips.
Commercial and cruise quays — holds and tanks on coasters during cargo work, and machinery-space piping on cruise ships.

context.h: Ships that never berth: inspection drivers at the Skaw
p: Ships calling at Skagen harbour are subject to Paris MoU port state control carried out by the Danish Maritime Authority, but many of the vessels stopping off the point never come alongside in Denmark at all. For those ships the reasons for a gauging request come from elsewhere: a class recommendation due before the next port, a charterer's vetting, a buyer's inspection or the owner's own condition programme. Danish authorities have also stepped up checks on older tankers anchoring in the waters around Skagen, and a ship whose hull records are current and complete is better placed if she is boarded.

Bunker calls off Skagen bring together ships of every age and flag, and the questions owners ask about them are commercial as well as technical. Danish ports are EU ports, so the EU ETS from 2024 and FuelEU Maritime from 2025 apply to the voyages that end in them, and ships of 500 GT and above that call at them need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials. Ice is not a feature of the Skagen anchorage, but ships heading on to the northern Baltic in winter carry ice class, and an anchorage stop is a last chance to check the parts of the ice belt that sit above the waterline when the ship is in ballast.

jobs.p: Skagen jobs are mostly short and arranged at short notice, because the reason a ship stops here is usually fixed only days before she arrives. A superintendent learns that the ship will bunker off the point, a broker hears that a tanker will lie at anchor for a week, or a trawler owner books gauging for the days between two fisheries. We plan around the window the agent can confirm, prepare a scope the crew can make ready before the launch arrives, and send readings to the office as each space is finished. Longer stays at anchor allow more ambitious programmes, as long as the weather holds and the boarding stays safe.
list: Deck, hatch coaming and air-pipe gauging on a bulk carrier during a bunker stop, following a port state control comment at the previous port.
Pre-purchase gauging of ballast tanks and deck on a product tanker lying at anchor while her sale is negotiated.
On-hire condition gauging of a tanker waiting off Skagen before she starts a time charter.
Hull plating and refrigerated sea-water tank gauging on a pelagic trawler alongside between the herring and mackerel seasons.
Scrubber overboard piping readings on a container ship at anchor, taken while the system is shut down for the stop.

logistics: Aalborg Airport is the nearest airport with international flights; from Aalborg, trains run north to Frederikshavn and a local line continues to Skagen, or the team travels on by road. Copenhagen and Billund are the usual long-haul arrival points. Launches for the anchorage are booked by the ship's agent, who also handles boarding notifications, while the fishing and commercial quays are reached through the port's normal access arrangements. The team comes from India on Schengen visas, so owners who use Skagen stops regularly benefit from having visas in place before a particular call is fixed.

faqs.q: How long does a ship need to stay at the Skagen anchorage for gauging to be worthwhile?
faqs.a: A few hours is enough for a focused deck and air-pipe scope with one or two prepared ballast tanks. A full day allows a wider set of tanks, provided the crew empties and ventilates them in sequence. Tankers waiting for orders over several days can support a pre-purchase or on-hire programme. We size the scope to the time the agent confirms and put the critical readings at the top of the list.

faqs.q: What happens if the weather stops boarding off Skagen?
faqs.a: Launch transfers stop when the sea state makes the ladder unsafe, and easterly winds are often the main problem at the Skagen anchorages. If the ship's stay is long enough, the team waits ashore for a better window; if she has to sail, we agree with the superintendent whether to measure at the next port or rejoin the ship elsewhere. Readings already taken are reported in full, so nothing is lost.

faqs.q: Can tankers be gauged during a ship-to-ship transfer off Skagen?
faqs.a: Not during the transfer itself, when the crew is occupied with cargo operations under strict safety controls. Before or after the operation, while the tanker lies at anchor, segregated ballast tanks, void spaces and deck structure can be measured if the master and the ship's safety management system allow it. Cargo tanks remain closed unless the ship has been cleaned and gas-freed for entry.

faqs.q: Can a ship be gauged while she bunkers off Skagen?
faqs.a: Yes, with care. Bunkering is a controlled operation around the manifold and the fuel tanks, so the team keeps clear of it and works in ballast tanks, on the forward deck, in holds or on hatch covers while fuel is delivered. The master's permit system decides which areas are open, and the agent times the launch so that the team does not arrive alongside while the barge is mooring.

faqs.q: Is there a dry dock at Skagen for larger ships?
faqs.a: Not for large merchant ships. The shipyard in the harbour works on fishing vessels and smaller specialised craft, so merchant ships needing a docking after a Skagen stop usually go to Frederikshavn, Funen or a Baltic yard. A useful pattern is to gauge tanks and deck at the anchorage, send the readings to the yard as a steel estimate, then complete the shell and bottom once the ship is in dock.
